commands.desc: Authenticate wrangler with your Cloudflare account
commands.tooltip: Opens your browser for OAuth and stores the token locally so wrangler can act as you. Run this once per machine before deploying or managing resources. For headless or CI environments, skip it and export CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN instead. Pair with `npx wrangler whoami` to confirm the session works.

commands.desc: Revoke wrangler's Cloudflare OAuth access
commands.tooltip: Invalidates the OAuth token and deletes stored credentials from this machine. Any scripts relying on the session will need to log in again. Does not delete your Cloudflare account or its resources, only the local authorization.

commands.desc: Show the authenticated Cloudflare user and accounts
commands.tooltip: Prints your email, account memberships, and token permissions, which makes it the first command to run when auth fails. Non-zero exit and an error message mean you are not logged in. See also `npx wrangler auth token` to inspect the credential itself.

commands.desc: Show authenticated user info as JSON
commands.tooltip: Returns account and identity details machine-readable for scripts and CI checks. Exits with a non-zero status when not authenticated, so it doubles as an auth assertion. The plain `npx wrangler whoami` output is easier to read by eye.

commands.desc: Print the current Cloudflare auth token
commands.tooltip: Prints whichever credential wrangler resolves first: the CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN environment variable, an API key and email pair, or the OAuth token from `wrangler login`. Useful for feeding other tools and scripts. Add `--json` to also get the token type and to retrieve API key credentials.

commands.desc: Print auth token with type metadata
commands.tooltip: Returns JSON with the token and its type: api_token, oauth, or api_key. The api_key type (email plus key pair) is only available with this flag, since it is two values rather than one. Refresh happens automatically for expired OAuth tokens.

commands.desc: Scaffold a new Workers project directory
commands.tooltip: Creates a folder named my-worker with a Worker template, wrangler config, and package.json via the create-cloudflare CLI. Prompts you to pick a language and framework unless flags are given. A Worker is serverless JavaScript that runs at Cloudflare's edge, so there is no server to provision.

commands.desc: Scaffold a project accepting default answers
commands.tooltip: Answers yes to every interactive prompt, so the scaffold completes without input. Good for scripts and quick experiments. Uses the current directory name as the project name when NAME is omitted, as in `npx wrangler init --yes` from inside an empty folder.

commands.desc: Download an existing Worker from the dashboard
commands.tooltip: Fetches a Worker you already created in the Cloudflare dashboard into a local my-worker folder. Edits made in the dashboard after this snapshot are not synced back, so treat the CLI as the source of truth going forward.

commands.desc: Create a Worker with the C3 scaffolding tool
commands.tooltip: Runs C3, the create-cloudflare CLI, which asks which framework and template to use and optionally deploys immediately. npm create is shorthand that fetches the latest package each run, so you always get current templates. `npx wrangler init` delegates to this same tool.

commands.desc: Scaffold a Worker from a GitHub template
commands.tooltip: The --template flag takes any GitHub repo in owner/repo form, so you can start from cloudflare/templates examples or your own private template. The extra `--` separates npm's own flags from the ones passed to C3. Plain `npm create cloudflare@latest my-worker` uses the built-in template list instead.

commands.desc: Generate TypeScript types for your Worker
commands.tooltip: Writes worker-configuration.d.ts with an Env interface derived from your bindings plus Workers runtime types for your compatibility date. Bindings are the config lines that connect your Worker to KV, D1, R2, and other resources. This replaced the old cf-typegen command. Re-run it after editing wrangler.toml.

commands.desc: Authenticate wrangler via an API token env var
commands.tooltip: Lets wrangler authenticate without a browser, which is the standard pattern for CI, containers, and remote machines. Tokens starting with cfat_ are account-scoped API tokens; scopes decide what commands may run, so a DNS-only token fails on Workers operations. CLOUDFLARE_API_KEY plus CLOUDFLARE_EMAIL works as an alternative pair.

commands.desc: Open the wrangler documentation in a browser
commands.tooltip: Launches developers.cloudflare.com/workers/wrangler in your default browser for full command and configuration reference. Handy when a --help output is not enough. The docs cover config file options, bindings, and CI/CD auth setup.

commands.desc: Run your Worker locally in a dev server
commands.tooltip: Starts a local server on http://localhost:8787 that runs your Worker with the Miniflare simulator, with hot reload on save. Local state (KV, D1, R2) persists under .wrangler by default. Add --remote to use real production bindings instead.

commands.desc: Run the dev server on a custom port
commands.tooltip: Overrides the default port 8787 when it is taken or when you want a specific URL. Useful when several workers run at once on different ports. The value can also live in the wrangler config file.

commands.desc: Expose the dev server on all network interfaces
commands.tooltip: Binds the dev server beyond localhost so other machines, phone browsers, or containers on the network can reach it. The default binds to localhost only, which is safer. Pair with --port to pick the listening port, as in `npx wrangler dev --ip 0.0.0.0 --port 3000`.

commands.desc: Run the dev server against remote resources
commands.tooltip: Runs your Worker on Cloudflare's network using your real KV, D1, R2, and other bindings instead of local mocks. This is the closest preview of production behavior but touches live data, so avoid destructive code paths while testing. Plain `npx wrangler dev` stays fully local.

commands.desc: Trigger scheduled handlers from the dev server
commands.tooltip: Adds a /__scheduled route that fires your Worker's scheduled event handler (a cron trigger) so you can test it locally. Append a cron pattern to simulate timing, like /__scheduled?cron=*+*+*+*+*. Without this flag, scheduled events never fire in local dev.

commands.desc: Share your local dev server over a public tunnel
commands.tooltip: Creates a Cloudflare Tunnel that gives you a public trycloudflare.com URL pointing at your local dev server. Great for testing webhooks or showing work in progress. The URL dies when the dev process stops; use a named tunnel with --tunnel-name for a stable one.

commands.desc: Deploy your Worker to production
commands.tooltip: Bundles your code and uploads it as a new production deployment of the Worker named in wrangler.toml. The previous version stays available for rollback. Add --dry-run first to preview the bundle without publishing. Cron triggers and routes from config deploy with it.

commands.desc: Preview the deploy bundle without uploading
commands.tooltip: Builds the Worker exactly as deploy would and reports the bundle size and assets, then stops without publishing anything. Perfect for CI checks and for confirming config changes compile. When output looks right, drop --dry-run to ship it.

commands.desc: Deploy with minified JavaScript
commands.tooltip: Minifies the bundled Worker before upload, shrinking the artifact and often improving cold-start times. Runtime behavior stays identical, but stack traces reference mangled names, which complicates debugging. Combine with --outdir to keep the minified output for inspection.

commands.desc: Write the deploy bundle into a directory
commands.tooltip: Saves the bundled output to dist/ instead of only uploading it, so you can inspect or commit the exact artifact that shipped. Useful with --minify to review the minified code. The directory is written before the deploy step runs.

commands.desc: Delete a Worker and its resources
commands.tooltip: Permanently removes the Worker script, routes, cron triggers, and associated developer platform resources. There is no undo, and any domains pointing at it start failing. Add --dry-run to preview what would be deleted. Version history and deployments go with it.

commands.desc: Upload a Worker version without deploying
commands.tooltip: Creates a new version of your Worker on Cloudflare but leaves the current deployment untouched, so traffic keeps running the old code. Versions are immutable snapshots you can later promote with `wrangler versions deploy`. Attach --tag or --message to label the version.

commands.desc: Upload a Worker version with a tag
commands.tooltip: Tags the uploaded version so you can target it later by name instead of by opaque version ID, e.g. `wrangler versions deploy release-2026-08-01`. Tags are a naming layer over immutable versions. --message works the same way for a free-text note.

commands.desc: Deploy a previously uploaded Worker version
commands.tooltip: Promotes an uploaded version to become the active deployment immediately. The version ID comes from `wrangler versions list`. Because versions are immutable, this is the safe path for canaries: upload, test, then deploy. Add @percentage for gradual traffic shift, like 4d9c2b1af3e84a6d9b7c1e2f3a4b5c6d@25.

commands.desc: Gradually shift traffic to a new Worker version
commands.tooltip: Starts a gradual deployment where 25 percent of requests hit the new version and 75 percent stay on the current one, letting you watch metrics before going fully live. The percentage shorthand is version-id@percent. Follow up with a full deploy at @100 once the rollout looks healthy.

commands.desc: List the 10 most recent Worker versions
commands.tooltip: Shows recent version IDs, authors, creation times, and any tags or messages attached at upload time. Version IDs feed `wrangler versions deploy` and `wrangler rollback`. Add --json for script-friendly output.

commands.desc: List the 10 most recent deployments
commands.tooltip: Shows the deployment history of your Worker: what version went live, when, and who deployed it. A deployment is a version plus when it became active. Use this to find what is currently serving traffic before rolling back. Supports --json.

commands.desc: Roll back to the previous Worker version
commands.tooltip: Immediately creates a new deployment of the version uploaded before the current one, across all routes and domains. This is a live production change, so expect a brief traffic shift while it propagates. Local dev is unaffected. Pass a version ID positionally to roll back further, as in `npx wrangler rollback 4d9c2b1af3e84a6d9b7c1e2f3a4b5c6d`.

commands.desc: Roll back to a specific Worker version
commands.tooltip: Deploys the given version ID as the new active deployment, useful when the previous version is not the one you want. Grab the ID from `wrangler versions list`. Same caution as plain rollback: it changes production immediately, so confirm the ID first.

commands.desc: Deploy cron triggers defined in the config
commands.tooltip: Syncs the cron triggers from your wrangler config to the deployed Worker, so scheduled handlers fire at the configured intervals. A cron trigger is a schedule like every 10 minutes that invokes your Worker's scheduled handler. Run it after adding or editing schedules in wrangler.toml.

commands.desc: Stream live logs from a deployed Worker
commands.tooltip: Opens a live feed of console.log messages, exceptions, and request metadata for the deployed Worker named my-worker. Useful for debugging production without touching the dashboard. On high-traffic workers the feed may sample, dropping some entries. Stop with Ctrl+C.

commands.desc: Tail Worker logs as JSON lines
commands.tooltip: Emits each log entry as a JSON object instead of pretty-printed text, which pipes cleanly into jq or log pipelines. The plain --format pretty default is easier to read in a terminal. Other filters like --status and --search work the same way in both formats.

commands.desc: Tail only failed Worker invocations
commands.tooltip: Filters the live log stream to invocations that ended with an error, cutting through noise when hunting a production bug. Accepts ok, error, or canceled. Combine with --search to match text inside console.log messages.

commands.desc: Tail logs matching a text pattern
commands.tooltip: Shows only log entries whose console.log messages contain DB_TIMEOUT, handy when you know the failing code path. Combine with --status error to see just failed requests, or --method GET to filter by HTTP verb. Quote the pattern so the shell passes it as one argument.

commands.desc: Create or update a Worker secret
commands.tooltip: Prompts for a value and stores it as an encrypted secret bound to your Worker's runtime, so code reads it from the environment without the value ever appearing in source or the dashboard. Each put creates a new version and deploys it immediately. Secrets are the right home for API keys and tokens.

commands.cmd: npx wrangler secret put API_KEY --name my-worker
commands.desc: Set a secret on a specific Worker by name
commands.tooltip: Targets the Worker named my-worker instead of reading the name from wrangler.toml, which is what you need when running outside the project directory. Useful in scripts that manage several workers. The --name flag appears on most secret commands.

commands.cmd: echo "sk-live-9f2a" | npx wrangler secret put API_KEY
commands.desc: Set a secret from piped input
commands.tooltip: Feeds the secret value through stdin so the put runs non-interactively, the standard pattern for CI pipelines and scripts. The trailing newline from echo is stripped. For many secrets at once, prefer `npx wrangler secret bulk secrets.json`.

commands.desc: List secret names on a Worker
commands.tooltip: Prints the names of all secrets configured for the Worker in the current project. Values are never shown, only names, because secrets are write-only by design. Use this before deleting to confirm what exists.

commands.desc: Delete a secret from a Worker
commands.tooltip: Removes the secret and immediately deploys a new version without it, so code reading the variable gets undefined. Any feature depending on the secret breaks until a new value is set with `wrangler secret put`. There is no confirmation prompt, so be sure.

commands.desc: Set or delete many secrets in one request
commands.tooltip: Reads a JSON file like {"API_KEY":"abc","WEBHOOK_URL":"https://x"} and writes up to 100 secrets in a single call. A null value deletes that key. An .env file with KEY=VALUE lines also works, but deletion is not supported from .env. Without a file argument it reads stdin.

commands.cmd: npx wrangler kv namespace create GREETINGS
commands.desc: Create a new KV namespace
commands.tooltip: KV is Cloudflare's global key-value store for Workers, and a namespace is the container that groups keys. The command prints a namespace ID you must copy into wrangler.toml as a binding before code can use it. Run `npx wrangler kv namespace create GREETINGS --binding GREETINGS` to have wrangler update the config for you.

commands.cmd: npx wrangler kv namespace create GREETINGS --binding GREETINGS
commands.desc: Create a KV namespace and bind it in the config
commands.tooltip: Creates the namespace and automatically adds the binding to wrangler.toml, skipping the copy-paste step. A binding is the name your Worker code uses to reach the store, e.g. env.GREETINGS. Re-run `npx wrangler types` afterward to refresh the Env type.

commands.desc: List KV namespaces in your account
commands.tooltip: Shows every namespace with its ID and title, which is how you find the --namespace-id value for key commands when no binding exists. The ID is a long hex string, not the friendly name. Pipe through grep to filter by project.

commands.cmd: npx wrangler kv namespace delete GREETINGS --namespace-id 2f1b3c4d5e6f7a8b9c0d1e2f3a4b5c6d
commands.desc: Delete a KV namespace
commands.tooltip: Permanently deletes the namespace and every key inside it, with no recovery. This is the most destructive KV command, so confirm the ID is the right namespace first. Pass --skip-confirmation to bypass the prompt in scripts. Deleting is not the same as removing keys individually with `wrangler kv key delete`.

commands.cmd: npx wrangler kv key put greeting "Hello world" --namespace-id 2f1b3c4d5e6f7a8b9c0d1e2f3a4b5c6d
commands.desc: Write a key-value pair to KV
commands.tooltip: Stores the value Hello world under the key greeting in the namespace. The key and value are positional; the value can be any string up to 25 MiB. Keys propagate to Cloudflare's global edge within seconds. For file contents as the value, use --path instead.

commands.cmd: npx wrangler kv key put config.json --path ./config.json --namespace-id 2f1b3c4d5e6f7a8b9c0d1e2f3a4b5c6d
commands.desc: Write a file's contents as a KV value
commands.tooltip: Reads the value from ./config.json instead of the command line, which keeps large or multi-line payloads out of your shell history. The key is still positional, here config.json. Use --ttl or --expiration to make the entry expire, or --metadata to attach JSON metadata.

commands.cmd: npx wrangler kv key put coupon "SAVE20" --ttl 86400 --namespace-id 2f1b3c4d5e6f7a8b9c0d1e2f3a4b5c6d
commands.desc: Write a KV key with a time to live
commands.tooltip: Stores the key with --ttl 86400, meaning it auto-expires 86400 seconds (one day) after being written. --expiration works the same but takes an absolute Unix timestamp. Useful for sessions, coupons, and cache-like data. Expired keys simply read as missing.

commands.cmd: npx wrangler kv key get greeting --namespace-id 2f1b3c4d5e6f7a8b9c0d1e2f3a4b5c6d
commands.desc: Read a value from KV by key
commands.tooltip: Fetches and prints the value stored under greeting. A missing key reports an error rather than an empty value. Output is base64-encoded by default for binary safety; add --text to print raw text directly. See `wrangler kv key list` to discover available keys.

commands.cmd: npx wrangler kv key get greeting --text --namespace-id 2f1b3c4d5e6f7a8b9c0d1e2f3a4b5c6d
commands.desc: Read a KV value as plain text
commands.tooltip: Same as the plain get but prints the value decoded as UTF-8 text, which is what you want for JSON, HTML, and normal strings. Without --text, values come back base64-encoded, so binary-safe but not human-readable. Pairs with `wrangler kv key put` for round-tripping.

commands.cmd: npx wrangler kv key delete greeting --namespace-id 2f1b3c4d5e6f7a8b9c0d1e2f3a4b5c6d
commands.desc: Delete a key from KV
commands.tooltip: Permanently removes the greeting key and its value from the namespace. There is no undo, though the global cache may still serve a stale copy for a short window. Deleting a key that does not exist is not an error. For many keys at once, use `wrangler kv bulk delete`.

commands.desc: List all keys in a KV namespace
commands.tooltip: Prints every key in the namespace along with metadata such as size and expiration, and paginates automatically for large stores. Useful for auditing what is stored and for building a delete list for `wrangler kv bulk delete`. Values are not shown, only keys.

commands.desc: Upload many KV pairs from a JSON file
commands.tooltip: Reads a JSON array like [{"key":"a","value":"1"},{"key":"b","value":"2"}] and writes every pair in one command, far faster than looping key put calls. Each entry can add expiration_ttl or expiration for per-key lifetimes. Handy for seeding data or migrating stores.

commands.desc: Delete many KV keys from a JSON list
commands.tooltip: Takes a JSON array of key strings, like ["a","b","c"], and deletes them all in one call. Destructive with no undo, so generate the list from `wrangler kv key list` and review it before running. Compare with `wrangler kv bulk put` for the upload counterpart.

commands.cmd: npx wrangler kv namespace rename GREETINGS --new-name GREETINGS_V2
commands.desc: Rename a KV namespace
commands.tooltip: Changes the namespace title to GREETINGS_V2 while keeping the same ID and all stored keys, so existing bindings keep working. The old name is the positional argument. Confirm the change with `npx wrangler kv namespace list` afterward.

commands.desc: Create a new D1 database
commands.tooltip: D1 is Cloudflare's serverless SQLite database, and this provisions an empty one named my-db. The output includes a database_id you must add to wrangler.toml as a binding before your Worker can query it. Then create tables with `wrangler d1 execute my-db --file ./schema.sql`.

commands.cmd: npx wrangler d1 create my-db --location weur
commands.desc: Create a D1 database in a specific region
commands.tooltip: Pins the primary location with a location hint such as weur (Western Europe), wnam, enam, eaur, or apac, reducing latency for regional users. D1 replicates data globally regardless, but the hint sets the home region. Omit it to let Cloudflare choose.

commands.desc: List D1 databases in your account
commands.tooltip: Prints every D1 database with its name, ID, and version, which is how you confirm a database exists and find its exact name. Add --json for machine-readable output. Names feed every other `wrangler d1` command.

commands.desc: Show D1 database size and state
commands.tooltip: Reports the database's current size, number of tables, and health state, useful before deciding to back up or restore. Add --json for script consumption. Size creeping up is a sign to prune old rows.

commands.cmd: npx wrangler d1 execute my-db --command "SELECT * FROM users LIMIT 10"
commands.desc: Run SQL against a D1 database
commands.tooltip: Executes the quoted SQL against the local D1 database by default, printing the rows as a table. You must supply either --command or --file. Add --remote to hit the production database, and --json to get results as JSON instead of a table.

commands.desc: Run a SQL file against D1
commands.tooltip: Executes every statement in schema.sql, the usual way to create tables and indexes or apply ad-hoc changes. Multiple statements run in one call, which is handy for seeding. For tracked, versioned schema changes, prefer migrations: `npx wrangler d1 migrations apply my-db`.

commands.cmd: npx wrangler d1 execute my-db --remote --command "DELETE FROM sessions"
commands.desc: Run SQL against the production D1 database
commands.tooltip: The --remote flag targets the live production database instead of the local copy, so statements like DELETE FROM sessions take effect immediately. Destructive SQL here is irreversible without a restore, so test against local first. Consider `wrangler d1 time-travel restore` as your safety net.

commands.cmd: npx wrangler d1 migrations create my-db add-users-table
commands.desc: Create a new D1 migration file
commands.tooltip: Generates a timestamped SQL file in the migrations folder named for your change, e.g. 0001_add-users-table.sql, ready for you to edit. Migrations are versioned schema changes that D1 tracks as applied. Name them as a description of the change; the description is what makes history readable.

commands.cmd: npx wrangler d1 migrations list my-db
commands.desc: List unapplied D1 migrations
commands.tooltip: Shows which migration files exist and which have not been applied yet, so you know what `wrangler d1 migrations apply` is about to run. Applied migrations are recorded in a migrations table inside the database. Run this before applying to review pending changes.

commands.cmd: npx wrangler d1 migrations apply my-db
commands.desc: Apply pending D1 migrations locally
commands.tooltip: Runs every unapplied migration file against the local D1 database and prompts for confirmation first. A backup is taken automatically before applying, so you can recover. For production, use `wrangler d1 migrations apply my-db --remote`.

commands.cmd: npx wrangler d1 migrations apply my-db --remote
commands.desc: Apply pending D1 migrations to production
commands.tooltip: Applies the pending migration files to the live remote database, the real deployment step for schema changes. A backup is created automatically before applying, which you can restore via `wrangler d1 time-travel restore`. Review `d1 migrations list` first, since production data is at stake.

commands.cmd: npx wrangler d1 export my-db --remote --output backup.sql
commands.desc: Export a D1 database to a SQL file
commands.tooltip: Dumps the schema and data of the remote database into backup.sql, the standard way to take a portable snapshot or migrate off Cloudflare. --local exports the local copy instead, and --no-schema or --no-data narrows the dump. Restore it later by running the file with `wrangler d1 execute`.

commands.cmd: npx wrangler d1 time-travel info my-db
commands.desc: Show available D1 restore points
commands.tooltip: Lists the point-in-time restore bookmarks D1 keeps for your database, driven by automatic backups taken on migrations and writes. This is the recovery menu: pick a bookmark, then restore with `wrangler d1 time-travel restore`. Older points fall out of retention, so back up early for critical data.

commands.cmd: npx wrangler d1 time-travel restore my-db --timestamp 2026-08-01T12:00:00Z
commands.desc: Restore a D1 database to a point in time
commands.tooltip: Rewinds the database to the state it had at the given timestamp, overwriting everything written since. Destructive to current data, so confirm the timestamp with `wrangler d1 time-travel info` first and export a snapshot if you need the newer data. Prefer --bookmark over --timestamp for exact restore points.

commands.desc: Delete a D1 database
commands.tooltip: Permanently removes the database and all its data, including backups, with a confirmation prompt. Add --skip-confirmation to bypass it in scripts. Export first with `wrangler d1 export` if there is any chance you need the data again. This cannot be undone.

commands.cmd: npx wrangler r2 bucket create my-assets
commands.desc: Create a new R2 bucket
commands.tooltip: R2 is Cloudflare's S3-compatible object storage, and a bucket is its container for files. Creating my-assets gives you a place to store images, uploads, or backups with no egress fees. The command prints a binding hint for wrangler.toml, or pass --binding to have it added automatically.

commands.cmd: npx wrangler r2 bucket create my-assets --location WNAM
commands.desc: Create an R2 bucket in a specific region
commands.tooltip: Pins the bucket's storage region, where WNAM means Western North America; other values include ENAM, WEUR, EEUR, APAC, and OC. Region choice affects latency and pricing, so pick the one closest to your users. Buckets cannot move regions later, so decide before creating.

commands.desc: List R2 buckets in your account
commands.tooltip: Prints every bucket with its creation date and storage class, giving you an inventory of object storage across the account. Useful before deleting anything. The CLI has no object-listing command, so to see contents use `wrangler r2 bucket info` or the REST API.

commands.cmd: npx wrangler r2 bucket info my-assets
commands.desc: Show R2 bucket details
commands.tooltip: Reports the bucket's region, creation time, and object count, a quick health check before uploads or deletions. Add --json for script-friendly output. For per-object detail you must use the API, since the CLI offers no object list command.

commands.cmd: npx wrangler r2 bucket delete my-assets
commands.desc: Delete an R2 bucket
commands.tooltip: Permanently removes the bucket, but only if it is empty; R2 refuses to delete a bucket that still holds objects. Delete the contents first with `wrangler r2 object delete` or the API, then run this. There is no recycle bin, so export anything valuable first.

commands.cmd: npx wrangler r2 object put my-assets/logo.png --file ./logo.png
commands.desc: Upload a file to an R2 bucket
commands.tooltip: Uploads ./logo.png into the bucket as the object key logo.png. The object path is bucket/key, so my-assets/logo.png targets the my-assets bucket. Set --content-type to control the MIME type served to browsers; omit it and R2 guesses from the extension.

commands.cmd: npx wrangler r2 object put my-assets/report.pdf --file ./report.pdf --content-type application/pdf
commands.desc: Upload a file with an explicit content type
commands.tooltip: Same upload as the plain put but pins the Content-Type header to application/pdf, which matters when R2's guess would be wrong or when serving files directly to users. Other header flags like --cache-control and --expires control edge caching. --force skips the data catalog validation prompt.

commands.cmd: npx wrangler r2 object get my-assets/logo.png --file ./logo.png
commands.desc: Download an object from R2 to a file
commands.tooltip: Fetches the object at my-assets/logo.png and writes it to ./logo.png on disk. Without --file, output goes to stdout, which suits text but not binaries. Object paths always start with the bucket name. This is the CLI counterpart to `wrangler r2 object put`.

commands.cmd: npx wrangler r2 object delete my-assets/logo.png
commands.desc: Delete an object from R2
commands.tooltip: Permanently removes the object at my-assets/logo.png. There is no undo and no versioning by default, so a deleted asset breaks any URL or Worker serving it. --force skips the confirmation prompt for scripts. Double-check the bucket and key before running.

commands.desc: Create a new Queue
commands.tooltip: A Queue buffers messages between Workers so producers and consumers run independently. This creates an empty queue named my-queue. Tune --message-retention-period-secs to keep messages longer before they expire, and --delivery-delay-secs to hold them before first delivery.

commands.desc: List queues in your account
commands.tooltip: Prints every queue with its name and ID, useful for finding the exact queue name for other commands. Messages are not listed, only queues. --page paginates large accounts. See `npx wrangler queues info my-queue` for per-queue detail.

commands.desc: Show queue details and stats
commands.tooltip: Reports the queue's retention settings, delivery delay, and consumer configuration, helping you confirm settings before changing them. Messages are delivered to a consumer Worker in batches, and this shows how that pipeline is wired.

commands.cmd: npx wrangler queues consumer add my-queue my-worker
commands.desc: Attach a Worker as a queue consumer
commands.tooltip: Wires my-worker to consume messages from my-queue in batches. The consumer Worker's queue() handler processes each batch; without a consumer, messages pile up until retention expires. --batch-size and --batch-timeout control batch shape, and --message-retries sets retry count on failure.

commands.cmd: npx wrangler queues consumer add my-queue my-worker --batch-size 10 --message-retries 3
commands.desc: Configure batch size and retries for a consumer
commands.tooltip: Adds the consumer with batches of up to 10 messages and 3 retries per message before it is considered failed, tuning throughput and reliability together. A failed message can be routed to a dead-letter queue via --dead-letter-queue instead of being dropped. Adjust retries carefully: too many delays processing.

commands.desc: Drop all messages in a queue
commands.tooltip: Deletes every message currently waiting in the queue, which is destructive: anything not yet consumed is gone forever. Pass --force to skip the confirmation prompt in scripts. Use it to clear a poisoned queue or discard a bad batch, not as routine cleanup.

commands.desc: Delete a queue
commands.tooltip: Permanently removes the queue, its pending messages, and its consumer bindings. Producers sending to it start failing until the binding is removed from their config. Confirm no worker still references it before deleting. This cannot be undone.

commands.cmd: npx wrangler pages project create my-site
commands.desc: Create a Cloudflare Pages project
commands.tooltip: Pages is Cloudflare's static hosting platform, and a project groups deployments of one site. In wrangler 4.x you must create the project before the first `wrangler pages deploy`; older versions auto-created it. The command prints the project's pages.dev URL.

commands.cmd: npx wrangler pages project create my-site --production-branch main
commands.desc: Create a Pages project with a production branch
commands.tooltip: Sets which branch counts as production, so deployments from main update the live site while other branches get preview URLs. If you use git flow with a main branch, pass this explicitly; the default may surprise you. Preview URLs make every PR testable before merge.

commands.desc: List your Pages projects
commands.tooltip: Prints every Pages project with its name, subdomain, and latest deployment, a quick inventory of what is hosted. Add --json for scripting. Project names feed `wrangler pages deploy --project-name` and the REST APIs.

commands.cmd: npx wrangler pages project delete my-site
commands.desc: Delete a Pages project
commands.tooltip: Permanently removes the project, all its deployments, and its custom domains, taking the site offline. There is no undo. Export or redeploy anything you still need first. Custom domain DNS records should be removed separately in the dashboard.

commands.desc: Deploy a static build to Pages
commands.tooltip: Uploads everything in ./dist as a new deployment of the Pages project, which defaults to the project name from config or an interactive prompt. The command prints the production and preview URLs. Requires the project to exist first: run `npx wrangler pages project create my-site` once.

commands.desc: Deploy to a named Pages project
commands.tooltip: Explicitly targets the my-site project, which is required when you are outside the project directory or when the folder name does not match. Every deploy creates a new immutable deployment, so previous ones remain available in the dashboard for rollback.

commands.desc: Deploy to a non-production branch
commands.tooltip: Creates a preview deployment tied to the staging branch, reachable at a preview URL, without touching the live production site. Branch-based deploys mirror how git flow works when connected to a repo. Promote later by deploying the same build to the production branch.

commands.desc: Run a Pages site locally
commands.tooltip: Serves the ./dist directory locally with Pages Functions support, so you can test static assets and serverless functions together before deploying. Defaults to a localhost port; pass --port to change it. Functions run with the local runtime rather than hitting production.

commands.cmd: npx wrangler pages deployment list --project-name my-site
commands.desc: List Pages deployments
commands.tooltip: Shows every deployment for the project with its environment, branch, and URL, which is how you find a specific deployment ID or rollback target. Add --json for scripting, or --environment to filter production versus preview. Each entry is immutable.

commands.cmd: npx wrangler pages deployment tail --project-name my-site
commands.desc: Stream live logs from a Pages deployment
commands.tooltip: Livestreams console logs and errors from the project's Functions, defaulting to the latest production deployment. Pass a deployment ID or URL positionally to tail a specific one, and --environment preview for the preview alias. Useful when a function misbehaves only in production.

commands.desc: Delete a Pages deployment
commands.tooltip: Permanently removes one deployment from the project, typically a broken preview. Deleting the current production deployment takes the site offline, so verify the ID from `wrangler pages deployment list` first. This cannot be undone.

commands.cmd: npx wrangler pages secret put API_KEY
commands.desc: Set a secret for a Pages project
commands.tooltip: Prompts for a value and stores it as an encrypted secret the project's Functions can read from the environment, without exposing it in source control. Same write-only model as Worker secrets. List names with `wrangler pages secret list` and remove with `wrangler pages secret delete`.

commands.desc: Compile Pages Functions into a single Worker
commands.tooltip: Bundles the ./functions directory into one Worker file for inspection or deployment elsewhere, mirroring what Pages does automatically at deploy time. Pages Functions let you add serverless endpoints to a static site using file-based routing. Mainly a debugging and CI tool.

commands.cmd: npx wrangler pages download config my-site
commands.desc: Download a Pages project's config
commands.tooltip: Fetches the project's current configuration from Cloudflare into a local wrangler config, including compatibility settings and bindings. Useful when adopting an existing project that has no local config yet. Edit it and re-deploy to change behavior.

commands.desc: Verify a Cloudflare API token
commands.tooltip: Asks the API whether the token in $CF_API_TOKEN is valid and what it can do. Caveat: zone-scoped tokens can report invalid here even when they work fine on DNS endpoints, so treat a failure as a signal to test the real endpoint instead of assuming the token is dead. Every REST call below needs this Bearer header.

commands.desc: Look up a zone ID by domain name
commands.tooltip: A zone is Cloudflare's representation of a domain you manage, and most DNS and cache API calls need its ID. This filters zones by name and extracts the ID with jq. Once you have ZONE_ID, export it and reuse it across the record and cache commands.

commands.desc: List all zone names on the account
commands.tooltip: Returns every domain in the account as a plain list of names via jq, handy for inventory or feeding a loop. The unfiltered endpoint paginates at 50 zones per page; add ?per_page=50 or page parameters for larger accounts. Zone names are domain names like example.com.

commands.desc: List DNS records for a zone
commands.tooltip: Prints every DNS record in the zone with its name, type, and content, the first step before editing records. The record ID you need for updates and deletes is in .result[].id, not shown by this jq filter. DNS records map hostnames to IPs, mail servers, or text values.

commands.desc: List DNS records filtered by record type
commands.tooltip: Narrows the zone's records to one type, here A records that point hostnames at IPv4 addresses, and lists just their names. Swap type for CNAME, MX, TXT, or AAAA to audit other kinds. Useful before creating a record to check for conflicts.

commands.desc: Create a DNS record via the API
commands.tooltip: Adds an A record pointing www.example.com at 1.2.3.4. ttl 1 means automatic, and proxied true turns on the orange cloud, hiding the origin IP behind Cloudflare's proxy. Set proxied false for mail and verification records, which must not be proxied. The response contains the new record's ID.

commands.desc: Update an existing DNS record
commands.tooltip: Changes just the fields you send, here repointing the record to 5.6.7.8 while keeping its type, name, and proxied status. RECORD_ID comes from the list command's .result[].id. Propagation is near-instant through Cloudflare, so verify with a lookup right after.

commands.desc: Delete a DNS record
commands.tooltip: Permanently removes the record, so anything resolving through it stops working, including email if you delete an MX record by mistake. There is no undo; recreate it with the POST command if needed. Confirm RECORD_ID against `wrangler`-free list output before deleting.

commands.desc: Purge the entire cache for a zone
commands.tooltip: Wipes every cached asset for the zone, forcing Cloudflare's edge to refetch from your origin on the next request. Use it after origin content changes that bypass normal cache invalidation. It causes a short origin load spike as the cache refills. Prefer targeted purges when only a few files changed.

commands.desc: Purge specific files from the cache
commands.tooltip: Removes only the listed URLs from Cloudflare's cache, leaving everything else intact, which is cheaper for the origin than a full purge. The files array takes full URLs, not paths. Cache tags and hostname-based purges are also supported for bigger rollouts.

commands.desc: Switch the SSL mode for a zone
commands.tooltip: Sets how Cloudflare encrypts the hop to your origin: flexible (origin over HTTP), full, or full strict (origin cert must match). The value full fixes 525 handshake errors with origins that have valid but self-signed or mismatched certificates. Mode changes propagate across the edge in about 30 seconds.

commands.desc: List accounts the token can access
commands.tooltip: Returns the Cloudflare accounts your token is scoped to, which gives you the ACCOUNT_ID required by the Workers, R2, and Pages endpoints. Account IDs are 32-character hex strings. If this returns nothing, the token lacks account-level access and will also fail on account APIs.

commands.desc: List Workers scripts via the API
commands.tooltip: Lists every Worker script in the account, which the wrangler CLI does not offer in one flat view. The script IDs are the Worker names. A token scoped only to zone DNS fails here with an auth error, since Workers are an account-level resource.

commands.desc: List R2 objects via the API
commands.tooltip: The wrangler CLI has no r2 object list command, so this REST call is the way to enumerate a bucket's contents. It returns object metadata including key, size, and last-modified; the jq filter extracts keys. Paginate with the cursor field for large buckets. Requires an R2 read-capable token.

commands.desc: Add a custom domain to a Pages project
commands.tooltip: Attaches docs.example.com to the my-site Pages project, which is needed because wrangler 4.x dropped the pages domain add command. After adding, create the matching CNAME record in DNS pointing to the project's pages.dev host. The domain activates once validation completes.

commands.desc: Purge a Pages project's build cache
commands.tooltip: Clears the cached build artifacts for the Pages project, forcing the next deployment to rebuild from scratch. Use it when a build is stuck on stale cache or produces inexplicable output. The cache rebuilds automatically on the next deploy, so this is safe but slightly slower.

commands.desc: Authenticate with a Global API Key
commands.tooltip: Legacy auth for scripts that predates API tokens: X-Auth-Email plus X-Auth-Key instead of a Bearer token. Global API Keys, which start with cfk_, carry full account access, so guard them like passwords and prefer scoped tokens. Sending a cfk_ key as a Bearer token returns an auth error.

commands.desc: Expose a local server via a quick tunnel
commands.tooltip: cloudflared is Cloudflare's tunnel client, and this one-liner creates an instant public URL on trycloudflare.com pointing at your local server on port 3000, with no account or config required. The URL dies when the process stops. For persistent tunnels, use `cloudflared tunnel create` and `cloudflared tunnel run` instead.

commands.desc: Analyze your Worker's startup performance
commands.tooltip: Runs the Worker locally and reports bundle size plus a startup CPU profile, helping you find slow initialization before it hurts users. Output shows gzipped bundle size, active CPU time, and garbage collection overhead. Run it after changes to confirm startup stays fast.
